title: Learning design to support student-AI collaboration: perspectives of leading teachers for AI in education
extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers think student-AI collaboration should be designed and implemented in schools. The study responds to a perceived lack of guidance for integrating AI into classroom learning, especially when AI is positioned not just as a tool, but as an active collaborative agent in students’ learning processes.

Using semi-structured interviews with 10 Korean leading teachers in AI in education, the authors explore views on curriculum design, student-AI interaction, learning environments, and how collaboration with AI may evolve over time. The discussion covers learning goals such as higher-order thinking, problem solving, creativity, social and digital capacities, and subject-matter knowledge building; content such as interdisciplinary learning, authentic problems, and creative tasks; and assessment focused on processes and collaboration performance.

The teachers also emphasized the need for explicit instruction on AI principles, data literacy, debugging/error analysis, ethics, and everyday AI experiences, along with AI systems that provide instructional scaffolding and intuitive interfaces. They further argued for flexible classrooms, strong digital infrastructure, systematic policy support, teacher capacity building, collaborative school culture, and safe-to-fail environments. The paper concludes that SAC may evolve from learning about AI to learning from AI and eventually learning together with AI in broader learning ecosystems.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative interview study, so it has some methodological rigor but does not provide causal evidence on student outcomes. It is useful for implementation and design hypotheses, not for establishing effectiveness of AI interventions in K-12 science reasoning.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report measured impact on student outcomes, effect sizes, or causal comparisons, so there is no demonstrable impact estimate to retain. Its contribution is mainly about narrower implementation conditions: interdisciplinary/authentic tasks, teacher mediation, process-oriented assessment, safe-to-fail culture, strong digital access, and explicit safeguards against blind reliance on AI.

finding.finding_summary: This is a qualitative interview study with 10 Korean leading teachers (n=10), not a causal comparison study of an AI tool. It reports proposed implementation conditions for student-AI collaboration rather than effects on student science reasoning outcomes, and it provides no delayed post-tests, transfer tasks, subgroup analyses, or quantitative fidelity estimates.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about curriculum, interaction, environment, and policy needs for student-AI collaboration

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed AI-supported learning should build higher-order and durable skills such as critical thinking, creativity, problem solving, collaboration, and data literacy, but these are expectations and design claims rather than measured effects. The paper cites prior studies, but this study itself reports no experimental outcome data, no delayed post-test, and no transfer task evidence.
finding.measure: Interview-coded expectations about higher-order thinking, collaboration, and AI/data literacy goals
